analysis.one_liner: Lets the President appoint DC's attorney general without Senate confirmation, replacing one voters elect.
analysis.headline: The House Oversight Committee approved the bill 25-20 on September 10, 2025, and it now sits on the House calendar awaiting a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites DC's Home Rule Act so the President, not DC voters, appoints the District's Attorney General. The appointee serves at the President's pleasure, needs no Senate confirmation, and the current elected Attorney General's term ends the day the bill becomes law. The office prosecutes local crime in the nation's capital and can sue the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: The President and the administration. They would gain direct, unconfirmed, at-will control over DC's chief law enforcement officer — the official who decides which crimes to prosecute locally and who can bring lawsuits against federal actors. There would be no Senate check, no fixed term independent of the White House, and no election for DC residents to remove the officeholder.

how_it_helps.text: The bill vests appointment of the DC Attorney General in the President, with the appointee serving at the President's pleasure and requiring no Senate confirmation.
The Attorney General's term would coincide with the President's term, tying the office directly to each administration.
The term of the person currently serving as elected Attorney General terminates on the day of enactment, handing the office over immediately.

analysis.who_pays: DC voters. They lose the right to elect their top local prosecutor, an office that under current DC law is chosen by them for a four-year term. The current elected officeholder is removed without a transition, and the office becomes answerable to one person — the President — rather than to residents, a Senate confirmation process, or any fixed term.
analysis.who_pays_short: DC voters and the elected AG

drawbacks.text: Under current DC law, the Attorney General is elected by DC voters for a four-year term, so the bill abolishes an election residents currently hold.
The bill removes every independent check on the office: no election, no Senate confirmation, no fixed term, and service at the President's pleasure.
The current Attorney General's term ends the day of enactment with no transition period, which could disrupt ongoing prosecutions and cases the office is handling.

Supporters' strongest argument is that the Constitution gives Congress broad authority over the federal district, and the federal government has a legitimate interest in who prosecutes crime at the seat of government. But that interest does not require eliminating elections, confirmation, and fixed tenure all at once.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits accrue entirely to whoever holds the presidency: at-will, unconfirmed control over local law enforcement in Washington, DC. The costs fall on roughly 700,000 DC residents, who lose both their vote for the office and, immediately, the officeholder they chose. Even a reader sympathetic to the federal government's interest in the District should notice that the bill bundles four separate removals of accountability — election, confirmation, term limits, and for-cause protection — into one change.

outcome.mechanism: The House Oversight Committee approved it 25-20 and placed it on the House's calendar, but the full House has not voted and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Pat Fallon (R-TX) introduced the bill on September 8, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
The committee held a markup on September 10, 2025, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a 25-20 roll-call vote.

On September 30, 2025, the committee reported the bill as amended (H. Rept. 119-316) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 270 — the list of bills awaiting a possible House floor vote.
Rep. Clay Higgins of Louisiana was added as an additional sponsor when the bill was reported.
No floor vote has occurred, and Congress remains in session through January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained anything concrete: the bill has not passed, and DC voters still elect their Attorney General. The bill's backers — its sponsors and the committee majority that reported it — have moved it one step from the floor, while DC residents have lost nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DC voters, so far — it hasn't passed

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and the bill's only cosponsor are Republicans, and the committee approved it 25-20 in a roll call; no floor vote has taken place yet to show the full House's split.

industries.industry: The presidency and executive branch leadership
industries.note: The President would gain at-will, unconfirmed control over DC's chief prosecutor — the office that handles local prosecutions and can sue federal actors — with no election, confirmation, or fixed term to constrain that control. The bill's gain for the White House is exactly what DC residents lose.

industries.industry: DC's Office of the Attorney General (local elected legal office)
industries.note: The office would stop being an independently elected local institution and become a presidential appointeeship; the current elected officeholder's term is terminated on enactment day. An independent local prosecutor is a direct check on both local and federal misconduct, so residents lose that check too.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Union Calendar awaiting House leadership action. Bills at this stage rarely reach the floor without leadership scheduling, and this one has only one cosponsor and no floor vote so far. A likelier path, if any, is as a provision attached to a District of Columbia appropriations bill; otherwise it will probably sit until the session ends without a vote.
